Satellite photo in, map out

satellite photo
map
In: an aerial photo taken from above.
Out: a map with roads, buildings and parks in flat colours.

01 · Satellite → map · the data
The Maps dataset
one file = one pair: 1,200 × 600 pixels
left half: satellite 600 × 600
right half: map 600 × 600
From the Pix2Pix paper. Google Maps views of New York City.
1,096 training pairs. 1,098 validation pairs, kept aside to check the model.
Each file holds both images of one pair, side by side.
Cut a file down the middle → input and target.
Why we need both halves in one file: a photo and its map can never get mixed up.

01 · Satellite → map · why this task
Why this task teaches well
1
Real: city photos, not a toy dataset.
2
Paired: a pixel-match target exists for every photo.
3
Visual: a broken road or a wrong colour is easy to see.
4
Two directions: satellite → map and map → satellite.
5
Famous: the showcase task of the Pix2Pix paper.
⇅
Why we need a task like this: we can test every part of Pix2Pix and judge the result by eye.
Unit 5 · 6 / 45
01 · Satellite → map · two directions
Two directions, two difficulties
Satellite → map
Job: pull out meaning: where are the roads and buildings?
Usually good: they are clearly visible in the photo.
Hard part: the exact map colours.
Map → satellite
Job: invent texture the map does not show.
Tree tops from green blobs, roofs from orange blocks.
Harder: results are often blurrier.
Why we need to compare the directions: the less the input shows, the more G must invent.

02 · U-Net + PatchGAN · the choice
Paired data, so Pix2Pix
Story so far: We have pairs. Now: pick the networks.
Generator: U-Net
Skip connections keep positions.
Unit 4 · advanced encoder-decoder
Discriminator: PatchGAN
Judges local texture, patch by patch.
Unit 4 · a grid of scores
Loss: GAN + pixel match
BCE (binary cross-entropy) or LSGAN (least squares GAN)
+ λ × L1, with λ = 100
L1 = average pixel gap between G’s map and the real map. λ = 100 → matching the real map is G’s main job.
Why we need Pix2Pix here: the data is paired, so every photo has an exact target map.

02 · U-Net + PatchGAN · U-Net
Why U-Net fits maps
satellite in
map out
128 × 128
64 × 64
32 × 32 …
128 × 128
64 × 64
… 32 × 32
bottleneck
1 × 1
skips: WHERE things are
bottleneck: WHAT the area is
Roads and buildings sit at exact positions in the photo. The map must put them at the same positions.
Skips carry “a road HERE, a building THERE”.
Bottleneck carries “this area is residential, that one is a park”.
Why we need U-Net for maps: together, skips and bottleneck give the right content in the right place.

Roads are thin lines that must connect. A broken road makes a bad map.
PatchGAN gives one score per patch, not one per tile.
The patch with the gap scores 0.2 → fake. The other 15 patches score 0.7 to 0.9.
G is told exactly where to fix the road.
Why we need a patch-by-patch judge: one small break is easy to spot locally.

03 · The unpaired problem · two piles
What if there are no pairs?
Story so far: Pix2Pix needs matching pairs. Now: two piles with no pairs.
Domain A: horses
horse 1, horse 2, horse 3 …
Domain B: zebras
zebra 1, zebra 2, zebra 3 …
✗ no horse matches any zebra
A domain is one kind of image: A = horses, B = zebras.
Horse 1 has nothing to do with zebra 1. They are two separate collections.
Maps too: satellite photos of some cities, maps of different cities.
Why we need unpaired translation: matching pairs are expensive to make and often impossible to get.

03 · The unpaired problem · the danger
The danger: ignore the input
horse running in a field
G_AB
zebra standing in a zoo
D_B
“real zebra” ✓
In: a horse running in a field.
Out: a zebra standing in a zoo.
D_B, the judge of zebras: “a real zebra” ✓
Pose, background, composition: all lost ✗
Why we need an extra rule: G needs a reason to keep the content and change only the style.
Unit 5 · 15 / 45
04 · Cycle consistency · the idea
The trick: go there and back
Story so far: G can ignore its input. Now: a check that forces it to keep the content.
real horse
G_AB
zebra
G_BA
horse again
should match: returned horse ≈ original
G_AB: horse → zebra (domain A → domain B)
G_BA: zebra → horse (domain B → domain A)
CycleGAN: Zhu et al., ICCV (International Conference on Computer Vision) 2017
Why we need the round trip: the original horse becomes the target, so no pair is needed.
Unit 5 · 16 / 45
04 · Cycle consistency · four networks
Two GANs in one
GAN 1
real horse
G_AB
fake zebra
D_B
“is this a real zebra?”
GAN 2
real zebra
G_BA
fake horse
D_A
“is this a real horse?”
GAN 1: G_AB makes zebras, D_B judges them.
GAN 2: G_BA makes horses, D_A judges them.
Each D also sees real images of its own domain.
Why we need two GANs: the round trip needs a way back, and each direction needs its own judge.
Unit 5 · 17 / 45
04 · Cycle consistency · two cycles
Forward and backward cycles
Forward
real horse
G_AB
fake zebra
G_BA
rebuilt horse
vs real horse: |rebuilt − real|
Backward
real zebra
G_BA
fake horse
G_AB
rebuilt zebra
vs real zebra: |rebuilt − real|
|rebuilt − real| = the pixel gap, averaged over all pixels (L1).
Why we need both cycles: each generator is checked as the first step and as the way back.
Unit 5 · 18 / 45
04 · Cycle consistency · why it works
Why the round trip keeps content
Keeps the content ✓
Only stripes added → G_BA can undo them.
Rebuilt horse ≈ real horse → small cycle loss.
Changes the pose ✗
Pose and background changed → G_BA cannot undo it.
Rebuilt horse ≠ real horse → cycle loss goes up.
So G_AB changes only what it must: stripes and colour.
Without the cycle, G_AB could map every horse to the same zebra.
Why we need the cycle loss: undoing a change is only possible if the content was kept.
Unit 5 · 19 / 45
05 · CycleGAN’s losses · overview
Four losses work together
Story so far: The round trip keeps content. Now: all the losses together.
1
GAN loss A → B
Fake zebras must look real to D_B.
2
GAN loss B → A
Fake horses must look real to D_A.
3
Forward cycle
horse → zebra → horse = the original horse
4
Backward cycle
zebra → horse → zebra = the original zebra
Why we need all four: the GAN losses make outputs look real, the cycle losses keep the content.
Unit 5 · 20 / 45
05 · CycleGAN’s losses · the formula
The total loss
L_total = L_GAN(G_AB, D_B) + L_GAN(G_BA, D_A)
+ λ_cyc × L_cycle + λ_id × L_identity
L_cycle = |G_BA(G_AB(a)) − a| + |G_AB(G_BA(b)) − b|
forward cycle + backward cycle
a = a real horse, b = a real zebra.
|…| = average pixel gap (L1).
λ_cyc = 10: the weight of the round-trip check.
λ_id = 5, half of λ_cyc: an optional identity term.
Why we need the weights: with 10 against 1, the round-trip check counts far more than looking real.
Unit 5 · 21 / 45
05 · CycleGAN’s losses · worked example
One generator step by hand
Given (one horse a, one zebra b): D_B(G_AB(a)) = 0.6 D_A(G_BA(b)) = 0.3 cycle gaps: horse 0.05, zebra 0.07 identity gaps: 0.04, 0.06 λ_cyc = 10, λ_id = 5 GAN part (LSGAN) = (score − 1)²
1
GAN A → B: (0.6 − 1)² = 0.16
2
GAN B → A: (0.3 − 1)² = 0.49
3
Cycle: 0.05 + 0.07 = 0.12 × λ_cyc 10 = 1.20
4
Identity: 0.04 + 0.06 = 0.10 × λ_id 5 = 0.50
5
L_G = GAN 0.16 + GAN 0.49 + cycle 1.20 + identity 0.50 = 2.35
The cycle part is 1.20 of 2.35: the biggest share.
Why we need these weights: they make keeping the content G’s main job.
Unit 5 · 22 / 45
05 · CycleGAN’s losses · identity
Identity loss: leave it alone
real zebra b
G_AB
G_AB(b): unchanged
L_identity = |G_AB(b) − b| + |G_BA(a) − a|
Give G_AB a zebra, already in domain B → it should change nothing.
It helps keep colours: without it, a sunset horse can become a green-tinted zebra.
Optional: weight λ_id = 5; used e.g. for photo ↔ painting.
Why we need identity loss: it stops G from changing colours it should leave alone.
Unit 5 · 23 / 45
05 · CycleGAN’s losses · LSGAN
LSGAN: a softer judge
BCE (Unit 1)
LSGAN: least squares GAN (Mao et al., 2017)
D on a real image x
−log D(x)
(D(x) − 1)²: push the score to 1
D on a fake G(z)
−log(1 − D(G(z)))
D(G(z))²: push the score to 0
G on its fake
−log D(G(z))
(D(G(z)) − 1)²: push the score to 1
Worked: D says 0.6 on a fake.
G loss = (0.6 − 1)² = 0.16
More stable training than BCE.
Still pushes fakes that fool D but sit far from the real images.
Smoother gradients → smoother images.
Why we need LSGAN: squared gaps keep pushing every fake towards real, so training is steadier.
Unit 5 · 24 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s parts · generator
Generator: ResNet, not U-Net
Story so far: We have the losses. Now: the networks that make CycleGAN work.
U-Net (Pix2Pix)
Skip connections copy positions straight across.
Suits aligned tasks: edges → photo, satellite → map.
The input’s layout maps directly onto the output’s.
ResNet (CycleGAN)
Residual blocks change features but keep their size.
Suits style changes: horse → zebra.
Horse and zebra: same shape, different texture.
ResNet’s generator learns: output = input + changes.
Why we need a ResNet generator: CycleGAN must keep the whole picture and change only its style.
Unit 5 · 25 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s parts · ResNet generator
Inside the ResNet generator
Sizes are written channels × height × width.
1 · Down-sample: 3 layers
input
3 × 256 × 256
64 × 128 × 128
128 × 64 × 64
256 × 64 × 64
2 · 9 residual blocks at the small size (6 in smaller versions)
256 × 64 × 64 in → 256 × 64 × 64 out, in every block
all the translation work happens here
3 · Up-sample: 3 layers back to full size
256 × 64 × 64
128 × 128 × 128
64 × 256 × 256
output
3 × 256 × 256
Why we need the small middle: the blocks work on 64 × 64 maps, 16 times fewer positions than 256 × 256.
Unit 5 · 26 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s parts · residual block
A residual block: input + changes
skip: x goes straight to the +
input x
conv → norm → ReLU → conv → norm
learns the changes
+
output = x + changes
Each block’s output = its input + what it learned to add.
G learns only the horse → zebra difference: stripes, colour.
Pose, background, shape: change ≈ 0, so they pass straight through.
One feature value (illustrative)
Stripe area: x = 0.40, change −0.30 → output 0.10
Background: x = 0.40, change 0.00 → output 0.40
Only the stripe area moved.
Why we need residual blocks: learning a small difference is easier than redrawing the whole image.
Unit 5 · 27 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s parts · normalisation
InstanceNorm, not BatchNorm
BatchNorm (Unit 1)
Averages over the whole batch of images.
InstanceNorm
Normalises each image on its own.
image (illustrative)
values, mean
BatchNorm: − batch mean 0.5
InstanceNorm: − its own mean
dark horse
0.1, 0.2, 0.3 → 0.2
−0.4, −0.3, −0.2
−0.1, 0.0, 0.1
bright horse
0.7, 0.8, 0.9 → 0.8
0.2, 0.3, 0.4
−0.1, 0.0, 0.1
BatchNorm: the dark horse’s result depends on the bright horse.
InstanceNorm: each horse is centred on its own mean.
Why we need InstanceNorm: every image has its own style, so each is normalised alone (Ulyanov et al., 2016).
Unit 5 · 28 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s parts · discriminators
Two PatchGAN judges
fake zebra
from G_AB
D_B
fake horse
from G_BA
D_A
Each judge: a 70 × 70 PatchGAN, one score per patch (green = looks real, orange = looks fake).
D_B: “is this a real zebra?” D_A: “is this a real horse?”
Pix2Pix D sees input + output stacked: 3 + 3 = 6 channels.
CycleGAN D sees the output only: 3 channels.
Why D sees one image: there is no paired input to compare with, so D only asks “does this look real?”
Unit 5 · 29 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s training · replay buffer
Replay buffer: remember old fakes
G_AB
new fake zebra
buffer
50 recent fake zebras
new or old fake
D_B
Problem: D sees only the newest fakes. It forgets old ones.
G can slide back to an old trick that D no longer catches.
1
First 50 fakes: stored, and passed to D as they are.
2
Buffer full: each new fake gets a 50 / 50 coin flip.
3
Heads: D gets a random old fake; the new one takes its slot.
4
Tails: D gets the new fake. So about half of D’s fakes are old.
Why we need a replay buffer: mixing in old fakes keeps D able to catch G’s old tricks.
Unit 5 · 30 / 45
06 · CycleGAN’s training · the recipe
The CycleGAN recipe
G_AB, G_BA
ResNet generators, 9 residual blocks
D_A, D_B
70 × 70 PatchGAN
losses
LSGAN (least squares GAN) + cycle L1 (λ_cyc = 10) + identity L1 (λ_id = 5)
optimiser
Adam, learning rate (lr) 0.0002, betas (0.5, 0.999), batch size 1
schedule
200 epochs: lr 0.0002 for 100, then linear decay to 0
extras
replay buffer 50 · InstanceNorm everywhere · resize 286 → crop 256, flip
Given: lr falls in a straight line from 0.0002 at epoch 100 to 0 at epoch 200. lr at epoch 150?
1
Decay epochs done: 150 − 100 = 50 of 100
2
Fraction left: 1 − 50 ÷ 100 = 0.5
3
lr = 0.0002 × 0.5 = 0.0001
Why we need the decay: a steady pace first to learn, then smaller steps to fine-tune.

07 · Paired vs unpaired · the key difference
One difference changes everything
Key difference: is there a target image for each input?
Paired → yes, a target exists
Pixel match (L1) to the target
U-Net G: skips copy positions
D checks the pair: input + output
Unpaired → no target
Cycle check: there and back
Second generator G_BA to undo G_AB
ResNet G: edits style, input + changes
D sees one image only
Why we need different architectures: the data decides what can be checked, and the networks follow.

Satellite → map without pairs
Given: 1,000 satellite photos of some cities. 1,000 maps of different cities. No photo has a matching map.
CycleGAN can still learn it: the cycle keeps the content of each photo.
Pix2Pix, with pairs
L1 pixel match to the real map.

CycleGAN, without pairs
Roads roughly right: they may shift, wiggle or break.
Colours may not follow the map rules.
Why we need pairs when we can get them: only a pixel match pins every road to its exact position.

Where CycleGAN is used
Style
photo → Monet

photo → Japanese woodblock
Animals
horse → zebra
Seasons and light
summer → winter
day → night
Domain adaptation
simulated → real images, to train robots

Common thread: no pairs, same content, new look.
Why we need CycleGAN here: nobody has the same scene photographed in both domains.
Unit 5 · 36 / 45
07 · Paired vs unpaired · limits
Where CycleGAN fails
1 · Shape changes
Horse → zebra works: same shape.
Cat → dog fails: different body proportions.
2 · Geometry
It can’t rotate, resize or restructure objects.
Only texture, colour and style change.
3 · Very different domains
Photo → abstract art: too far apart.
The cycle assumes shared content.
4 · Collapse
It may add the same pattern everywhere.
“Put stripes on everything.”
Why it matters: CycleGAN edits the look, not the layout; pick tasks that keep the shapes.

Unit 5 · 40 / 45
08 · The whole journey · what changed
What changed, and why
Losses
BCE: unstable
Wasserstein: stable gradients
+ gradient penalty: no clipping
+ L1 pixel match: exact for pairs
+ cycle: content without pairs
LSGAN: smoother than BCE
Architectures
linear layers: blurry
DCGAN: sharper, spatial
InstanceNorm: per-image
StyleGAN AdaIN: controllable
U-Net: keeps fine detail
ResNet G: input + changes
Evaluation
“looks good”: not repeatable
IS: quality + variety
FID: the standard
per-group FID: finds hidden bias
BCE: binary cross-entropy · AdaIN: adaptive instance normalisation · IS: Inception Score
The adversarial idea never changed: G tries to fool D, D tries to catch G.
Why it matters: each step fixed one specific problem of the step before.

What comes next
Diffusion models
DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney.
GANs led image generation until about 2022.

08 · The whole journey · final check
Final check
1
200 paired sketches and photos. Which model, which loss?
Pix2Pix: GAN loss + 100 × L1 pixel match
2
5,000 horse and 5,000 zebra photos, unpaired. Which model, which key loss?
CycleGAN: the cycle-consistency loss keeps the content
3
Great faces, but only light-skinned ones. What is wrong, and how do you detect it?
Bias from the data: compute FID per group
4
Why U-Net in Pix2Pix but ResNet in CycleGAN?
Aligned task: copy positions. Style change: output = input + changes.
5
Share medical data without identifying patients. Which technique?
Train with DP-SGD (differential privacy), or PATE-GAN
6
FID: is lower or higher better?
Lower: fakes closer to the real images
Why it matters: each answer picks the right tool for one real situation.
